definition: The distance an object travels per unit time, $v = \frac{s}{t}$, usually in m/s; a scalar, so it has no direction.
Speed in a given direction; a vector, so two objects with the same speed moving in different directions have different velocities.
The total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any stops; it is not, in general, the mean of the starting and final speeds.
The total length of the path an object travels, in m; a scalar, so it has no direction.
A graph of distance travelled (vertical axis) against time (horizontal axis); its gradient is the speed, so a horizontal line means at rest and a straight sloping line means constant speed.
A graph of speed (vertical axis) against time (horizontal axis); the area under it is the distance travelled (Extended: for motion in a straight line, its gradient is the acceleration).
The steepness of a straight line: the change in the vertical quantity divided by the change in the horizontal quantity, found from two points on the line far apart.
The change in velocity per unit time, $a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, in $\text{m/s}^2$; a vector.
A negative acceleration, taking the direction of motion as positive: the object's speed decreases.
The acceleration $g$ of an object falling with no air resistance; near the Earth's surface it is approximately constant, about $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$, whatever the object's mass.
The constant velocity an object falling through air or a liquid reaches when the forces on it balance, so the resultant force on it is zero; in air, this is when the air resistance equals its weight.
